sec.title: Background
sec.p: The translational study of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell function, persistence, immunophenotype, and spatial localization after infusion is crucial for understanding factors that influence clinical outcomes. However, research has been limited by a lack of optimized tools to reliably detect CAR-engineered cells. To address this, we developed a novel platform to generate monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) targeting a linker peptide incorporated in single-chain variable fragments (scFvs) of most CAR constructs.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Using recombinant proteins and scFv linker peptides as immunogens, we generated murine mAbs against the Whitlow linker peptide, capable of binding cells expressing Whitlow linker-containing CARs in both fresh and formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissues. We evaluated these antibodies in multiple in vitro translational applications relevant to CAR T-cell research and manufacturing.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: We identified five unique mAbs reactive against the Whitlow linker and characterized their binding properties and three-dimensional structural conformation. One clone was evaluated in depth, demonstrating comparable capacity to identify CAR T cells in peripheral blood relative to other methods using anti-idiotype antibodies or recombinant CAR-target proteins. In contrast to these reagents, the anti-Whitlow mAb detects cells expressing Whitlow linker-containing CARs with different antigen specificities, including those harboring the widely employed anti-CD19 FMC63-derived scFv as well as other scFvs, such as those targeting B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA) or CD33. Importantly, the anti-Whitlow mAb identified CAR T cells in situ in archival FFPE tissues, and a DNA-barcoded format enabled their spatial characterization and immunophenotyping in highly multiplexed immunohistochemistry. We also assessed the functional consequences of antibody binding on CAR T cells in vitro and demonstrated the feasibility of anti-Whitlow mAb-mediated selective enrichment of CAR-expressing T cells for potential utility in manufacturing workflows.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Anti-Whitlow mAb clones exhibited distinct structural and functional properties that can be leveraged for multiple applications, providing versatile tools for detection, selection and manipulation of a broad range of clinical and preclinical CAR T-cell products.

sec.title: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

list-item.p: The translational study of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells within patient tissues is limited by the lack of broadly available reagents that reliably bind CARs across different clinical products, particularly in archival tissue samples.

We developed murine monoclonal antibodies that recognize the Whitlow linker sequence incorporated in most clinical CAR constructs, enabling detection and phenotypic characterization of different clinical CAR T-cell products. Importantly, we provide a detailed evaluation of their use to identify CAR-expressing cells in clinical specimens not only by flow cytometry but also by immunohistochemistry. Further, these antibodies also provide a versatile platform for CAR T-cell manipulation, and we explored their use for selective stimulation and CAR T-cell enrichment.

sec.title: HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY

list-item.p: Our detailed description of the discovery and characterization of these anti-Whitlow antibodies provides a foundation for broadly applicable tools that can accelerate preclinical and translational CAR T-cell research and improve clinical assay harmonization across the field. These reagents will facilitate standardized correlative studies across clinical applications of CAR-engineered cells and enable cross-platform analyses, including flow cytometry and spatially resolved investigations within the tumor microenvironment.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) are recombinant proteins that can be introduced into immune cells to induce effector functions directed to other cells expressing the target antigen. CAR T-cell immunotherapy can be remarkably effective for B-lineage neoplasms, revolutionizing the treatment of a subset of these hematologic malignancies.1,5 This success has spurred enthusiastic development of CAR-based cellular immunotherapies for other hematologic indications, solid tumors and autoimmune disorders.6,9

To be effective in cancer immunotherapy, CAR-engineered cells must traffic to and infiltrate the tumor microenvironment (TME), engage cognate antigen, proliferate, and lyse target cells. Analyses of the properties of CAR-expressing cells prior to infusion and their in vivo fate and function after infusion provide insights into the mechanisms governing patient outcomes, including treatment response and immune effector cell-associated toxicities.10,14 However, research efforts have been hindered by the inability to directly identify CAR-engineered cells, particularly those present in situ in archival tissue biopsies. Therefore, we sought to develop antibodies that specifically bind the CAR in both fresh and formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissues.

CARs comprise an extracellular antigen-binding domain fused to intracellular signaling components that determine a CAR-expressing cell’s response on target antigen engagement.15 The antigen-binding moiety is usually an antibody-derived single-chain variable fragment (scFv), consisting of heavy (VH) and light (VL) chains connected by a linker peptide. Commonly used linkers include glycine-serine linkers (eg, G4S linkers) and the Whitlow linker, a synthetic peptide that reduces scFv aggregation and enhances proteolytic stability.16 The Whitlow linker is incorporated into the CARs of numerous CAR T-cell products of different specificities, including those such as axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel), lisocabtagene maraleucel (liso-cel), brexucabtagene autoleucel (brexu-cel), and idecabtagene vicleucel (ide-cel) that are approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA). It is an attractive target for a CAR-binding antibody because it is the most frequently used linker in FDA-approved CAR T cells, is not restricted to a single scFv specificity, and is not present in unmodified human tissues. Herein, we describe the discovery and characterization of novel murine monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) designed for the specific identification, selection, and manipulation of T cells expressing a Whitlow linker-containing CAR.

sec.title: Anti-linker mAb generation
sec.p: Murine anti-linker mAbs were generated at the Fred Hutchinson (Fred Hutch) Antibody Technology Core Facility in Seattle, Washington. Full details about the mouse immunization strategy, hybridoma generation and high-throughput (HT)-flow cytometry screening are described in online supplemental methodology. Briefly, mice of various strains were immunized with Whitlow peptide, (G4S)4 peptide and/or a Whitlow linker-containing anti-CD19 FMC63 mAb-derived scFv (FMC63-Whitlow scFv) in native or fixed format. Splenocytes used for hybridoma generation were isolated from mice selected based on serologic reactivity to one or more of the immunogens. Hybridoma supernatants were screened for reactivity against the Whitlow peptide, FMC63-Whitlow scFv, and cells expressing Whitlow-containing CAR constructs using HT flow cytometry on the iQue cytometer (Sartorius). Hybridoma clones were isolated using a ClonePix colony picker (Molecular Devices) and IgG was purified using protein A affinity chromatography for flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry (IHC) screening.

sec.title: Surface plasmon resonance
sec.p: Binding kinetics were assessed in triplicate under non-regenerative conditions for recombinant antibodies using the LSA instrument (Carterra). Antibodies (0.08–9.0 µg/mL) were captured using a protein A/G sensor chip followed by flow of increasing concentrations of FMC63-Whtilow scFv recombinant protein, Whitlow peptide or (G4S)4 peptide in a fivefold (0.8–500 nM) or twofold (125–2,000 nM) dilution series. The equilibrium dissociation constant (KD) was determined by curve-fitting using a 1:1 Langmuir model in Kinetics Software (Carterra).

sec.title: Three-dimensional modeling of antibody structures
sec.p: Molecular models were generated for each anti-Whitlow mAb as an Fv alone and in complex with the Whitlow peptide using AlphaFold 3. Structural inference was run with 100 seeds and 5 diffusion samples per seed. Models were ranked by top interface predicted template modeling (TM)-score between the VH and Whitlow linker, and the models with the greatest confidence were analyzed with electrostatics visualized using the APBS plugin in PyMOL.

sec.title: CAR T-cell generation
sec.p: CARs were constructed to encode an scFv, IgG4 hinge extracellular spacer, CD28 transmembrane domain, and intracellular 41BB and CD3ζ sequences. The CAR was separated by a ribosomal skip sequence from a truncated (t) non-signaling transduction marker such as CD19 or epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR).2 7 17 CAR T cells were generated by lentiviral transduction of negatively selected T cells from healthy donors or Jurkat cell lines as previously described.2

sec.title: CAR T-cell isolation
sec.p: CAR T cells were isolated using two approaches. For flow cytometry-based isolation, cells were incubated with anti-linker, anti-CD19 or anti-EGFR antibodies and sorted for each marker using fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS; MA-900, Sony Biotechnology, San Jose, California, USA). Alternatively, magnetic bead-based CAR T-cell isolation was performed; cells were incubated with an allophycocyanin (APC)-conjugated antibody followed by anti-APC MicroBeads (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat# 130-090-855) and CAR T cells were isolated by magnetic separation according to the bead manufacturer’s protocol.

sec.title: Patient samples and clinical data
sec.p: Cryopreserved peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and archival tissue samples were obtained from patients who had received CAR T-cell therapy. All samples were collected after written informed consent in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approval by the Fred Hutch Institutional Review Board.

sec.title: Secondary flow cytometry screening and downstream testing
sec.p: Each mAb was fluorescently labeled using a FlexAble linker labeling kit (Proteintech, Cat# KFA543, KFA523) specific for each antibody isotype. In some assays, the 1B4A1 mAb was directly conjugated with a fluorophore as outlined in the text (BioLegend). Labeled antibodies were titrated to determine optimum dose based on optimal staining index between FMC63-Whitlow CAR T cells and untransduced T cells. The staining index was calculated using the formula: (mean fluorescence intensity (MFI)pos-MFIneg/2×SDneg).

Cell staining was performed using standard protocols, and the list of antibodies used is available in online supplemental table 1. Data were acquired on a BD Symphony or Celesta flow cytometer and analyzed using FlowJo V.10.8.1 (BD Life Sciences). For evaluation of CAR T cells in patient-derived peripheral blood, a gating strategy was established using isotype controls. A representative gating strategy is shown in online supplemental figure 1.

sec.title: Formalin fixation, embedding, and IHC
sec.p: To generate CAR T-cell pellets, defined mixtures of viable CAR T cells and untransduced cells were prepared in proportions as outlined in each figure. Cells were fixed in 10% neutral-buffered formalin for 48 hours, then dehydrated sequentially in 70% and 100% ethanol. After centrifugation, pellets were solidified in HistoGel (Epredia, Cat# HG-4000–012), wrapped in alcohol-saturated Bio-Wrap (Leica, Cat# 3801090), placed in cassettes, and paraffin-embedded using standard protocols.

FFPE tissue specimens were sectioned at 4 µm onto positively charged slides and baked at 60°C for 1 hour. For single-marker IHC, antigen retrieval was performed using Tris-EDTA buffer, pH 9 (Abcam, Cat# ab93684), at 95°C for 20 min. Purified anti-Whitlow or anti-CD19 (Origene #UM500071) mAbs were applied using an intelliPATH Stainer (Biocare Medical), followed by anti-mouse Fc secondary detection, visualization with 3,3′-diaminobenzidine chromogen, and hematoxylin counterstaining.

sec.title: Multiplex immunohistochemistry
sec.p: FFPE sections were stained on a Leica BOND Rx autostainer using the Opal multiplex immunohistochemistry assay (Akoya Biosciences) with the following modifications: additional high-stringency washes were performed after secondary antibody and Opal fluorophore applications using high-salt TBST (Tris-buffered saline with Tween, 0.05 M Tris, 0.3 M NaCl, 0.1% Tween-20, pH 7.2–7.6). Blocking was performed using TCT (Tris-casein-Tween) buffer (0.05 M Tris, 0.15 M NaCl, 0.25% casein, 0.1% Tween-20, pH 7.6±0.1). Primary antibodies were incubated for 1 hour at room temperature. Slides were counterstained with 4’,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI), mounted with ProLong Gold, and cured for 24 hours at room temperature in the dark. Imaging was performed on either the Akoya Vectra V.3.0 or PhenoImager HT automated imaging system. Images were spectrally unmixed using inForm software (Akoya Biosciences).

For the PhenoCycler Fusion assay, antibodies against Pax5, granzyme B (GzmB), and CD19 were barcoded in-house using cysteine modification as previously described,18 while the 1B4A1 mAb was site-specifically conjugated using click chemistry (BioLegend). Ki-67 and CD3 antibodies were purchased pre-conjugated with barcodes (Akoya Biosciences). A list of antibody clones and barcodes is provided in online supplemental table 2. FFPE tissue sections (5 µm) were mounted on poly-L-lysine–treated slides, baked, deparaffinized, and subjected to antigen retrieval using Tris-EDTA buffer, pH 9 (Abcam, Cat# ab93684) at 95°C for 20 min. Slides were stained with an antibody mix containing all barcoded antibodies. Fluorescent reporters purchased from Akoya Biosciences and Integrated DNA Technologies were used for detection. Automated antibody cycling, image acquisition, and reporter dissociation were performed on the PhenoCycler Fusion platform. Resulting QPTIFF images were uploaded to the EnableMedicine portal (enablemedicine.com) for downstream analyses.

Analyses were performed on two viable tumor sections from each biopsy. Cell segmentation was performed using the DeepCell algorithm based on DAPI nuclear stain with a dilation factor of 9.19 Leiden unsupervised clustering using MFI for each protein marker was performed to identify relevant lymphoma and T-cell type clusters. Clusters were then annotated based on marker expression using heat maps validated by overlay onto stained images, and the percentage of cells in each cluster was tabulated. Cell-by-cell interaction was established as the proportion of cells that shared a cell border in Voronoi diagrams.

sec.title: Jurkat reporter screening
sec.p: To evaluate the capacity of anti-Whitlow mAbs to activate CAR-expressing Jurkat nur77-GFP reporter cells, a 1:1 mix of CAR-transduced and untransduced cells was cultured in complete media (Roswell Park Memorial Institute (RPMI) 1640 with 10% fetal bovine serum and 0.71 mM L-glutamine supplementation) and plated in wells coated with anti-Whitlow mAbs, isotype antibodies or in complete media containing phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA)-ionomycin, K562 cells±surface tCD19, or phosphate-buffered saline (vehicle). After 4 hours of co-culture, the cells were stained with antibodies to the transgene expression marker (tCD19 or tEGFR) and analyzed by flow cytometry. CAR-expressing Jurkat nur77-GFP reporter cell activation was determined by calculating the percentage of transgene marker-expressing cells that also expressed green fluorescent protein (GFP). Transgene expression marker-negative cells served as an internal negative control for GFP gating.

sec.title: CAR T-cell stimulation assays
sec.p: CAR T-cell stimulation assays were performed by incubating primary human CAR T cells or untransduced T cells with in-solution or plate-bound anti-Whitlow mAbs for up to 7 days. Cytokine secretion was assessed by Luminex (Thermo Fisher) analyses of supernatants from each co-culture. Viable cell counts were assessed by AOPI staining and quantified using the Cellometer K2 fluorescent cell counter (Revvity). Cells were also stained for expression of activation markers and analyzed by flow cytometry, as described.20

sec.title: Statistical analyses
sec.p: Data were analyzed with Prism V.10 (GraphPad Software, Boston, Massachusetts, USA) or RStudio software (RStudio, Boston, Massachusetts, USA). Hypothesis tests were performed as indicated.

sec.title: Discovery of murine mAbs that bind the Whitlow linker incorporated in scFvs
sec.p: To generate Whitlow linker-binding mAbs, we immunized 16 mice using linker peptides alone or incorporated into the FMC63 scFv recombinant protein (figure 1), which confers the specificity of the CARs in axi-cel and liso-cel for CD19. Based on serological reactivity with immunogens, hybridoma pools were generated from the spleens of six of the immunized animals and plated into 384-well plates. After selection, supernatants from each hybridoma pool were screened for binding to Whitlow or (G4S)4 linker peptides alone or incorporated into scFv proteins in recombinant format or expressed on the surface of human T cells.

sec.p: Of 4,608 hybridoma pools, 105 (2.28%) were reactive against human FMC63-Whitlow CAR T cells, while 58 (1.26%) reacted with the recombinant Whitlow peptide alone and 12 (0.26%) bound Whitlow peptide expressed in recombinant FMC63 scFv monomers (online supplemental table 3). 16 candidate hybridoma pools were then subcloned to monoclonality and two subclones from each pool were evaluated by flow cytometry in a subsequent screen against primary human T cells engineered to express CARs with an FMC63 scFv incorporating either a Whitlow or (G4S)3 linker (FMC63-G4S). Supernatant from six hybridoma clones specifically stained Whitlow linker-containing CAR T cells. Sequencing of the VH and VL regions revealed that two clones were identical, resulting in five distinct anti-Whitlow mAbs. IgG was purified from the supernatants of these five hybridomas for subsequent studies.

sec.title: Novel anti-Whitlow mAbs bind human T cells expressing a Whitlow linker-containing CAR
sec.p: We compared the performance of each novel mAb in binding CAR T cells using a flow cytometry-based assay. The mAbs were labeled with a rapid high-affinity fluorescent labeling system and titrated to determine their optimal staining concentrations. We then evaluated their relative reactivity against CD19-directed CAR T cells generated from different healthy human donor T cells (n=3). All five mAbs bound to FMC63-Whitlow CAR T cells, but not to untransduced T cells nor those incorporating a FMC63-G4S CAR (figure 2A).

sec.p: To determine if these mAbs also bind to the Whitlow linker sequence when incorporated in scFvs other than FMC63, we tested them against healthy human donor CAR T cells expressing the 1H7 scFv, which targets the CD33 antigen frequently expressed in acute myeloid leukemia.7 Here too, all five mAbs demonstrated staining of 1H7-Whitlow CAR T cells, but not 1H7-G4S CAR T cells (figure 2B). Notably, the relative MFI of stained FMC63-Whitlow CAR T cells and 1H7-Whitlow CAR T cells differed between the five mAbs, potentially reflecting differences in antibody binding affinity, avidity or labeling efficiency.

To analyze the interactions between the binding domains of each mAb and the Whitlow linker peptide, we generated chimeric antibodies in which the murine variable domains were fused to human IgG1 constant regions and then tested them using an HT surface plasmon resonance (SPR) assay. The binding kinetics, presented in table 1, demonstrate the range of KD values for binding to recombinant FMC63-Whitlow scFv (0.1–3.4 µM) or the Whitlow peptide alone (0.11–0.96 µM). Three of the antibodies exhibited a two to four-fold higher affinity for the Whitlow peptide compared with FMC63-Whitlow scFv and one (1G2G2) showed no reactivity under the conditions tested. As expected, there was no observable binding to the (G4S)4 peptide. The affinity ranking of the recombinant antibodies toward the Whitlow peptide alone or contained within the FMC63 recombinant protein is 1H5b>1B4A1>1B3b≅1C3C3.

sec.p: To gain insight into the paratope region of the mAbs and how they interact with the Whitlow peptide, we generated three-dimensional molecular models for each mAb (online supplemental figure 2A). Overall, a conserved pattern of interaction can be seen with a negatively charged cleft between the variable domains for all mAbs, except for 1H5b, which displays a similarly sized negative island layered across the heavy chain. Docks for 1B3b, 1B4A1 and 1C3C3 were modeled with high confidence and suggest the negative cleft allows interaction with the Whitlow peptide through a bent conformation, optimizing contact and interaction (online supplemental figure 2B and C). Further, all the mAbs display a low net positive charge (≤3 for all mAbs), suggesting a low risk of positive charge-based polyreactivity (online supplemental figure 2D).

These data demonstrate that four mAbs—1H5b, 1B4A1, 1B3b, and 1C3C3 bind to epitopes within the Whitlow peptide sequence, providing novel reagents for the specific detection and identification of Whitlow-containing CAR T cells in patient samples.

sec.title: Novel anti-Whitlow mAbs accurately detect CAR-engineered T cells in clinical samples using flow cytometry
sec.p: Next, we sought to evaluate the potential of a novel anti-Whitlow mAb to detect CAR-expressing T cells in clinical blood samples using flow cytometry. We elected to use the 1B4A1 mAb for these assays because of its consistently strong and specific staining of cultured FMC63-Whitlow-containing and 1H7-Whitlow-containing CAR T cells generated from different healthy donors (n=3; figure 2; online supplemental figure 3). To minimize batch-to-batch variation and improve the precision of our measurements, we fluorescently labeled and titrated the 1B4A1 antibody using site-specific APC conjugation.

We prepared admixtures of FMC63-Whitlow CAR T cells in serial dilution with normal human PBMCs to simulate clinical peripheral blood samples from patients treated with CAR T-cell therapies and stained them with either APC-conjugated 1B4A1 or a commercial anti-FMC63 idiotype antibody. We observed a very strong correlation in the proportion of CAR T cells detected in these admixtures using the 1B4A1 anti-Whitlow linker mAb compared with the anti-FMC63 idiotype antibody (r²=0.9980, p<0.0001), without significant bias (figure 3A,B) and with minimal background (online supplemental figure 4). Assuming this background represents the limit of blank, the limit of CAR T-cell detection per sample is estimated to be 0.1% (limit of detection=mean of blank+3×SD of blank).

sec.p: To confirm the ability of the 1B4A1 mAb to specifically identify Whitlow linker-containing CAR T cells in clinical blood samples, we stained PBMCs isolated from patients (n=32) prior to lymphodepleting chemotherapy and at multiple time points following infusion of commercial CAR T-cell products. This approach enabled the capture of in vivo CAR T-cell kinetics, reflecting the varying frequencies of circulating CAR T cells during treatment. As anticipated, CAR T-cell counts assessed using the 1B4A1 mAb strongly correlated with those obtained using an anti-FMC63 idiotype antibody or recombinant target proteins (figure 3C–H; online supplemental figure 5). In blood from patients treated with CAR T cells lacking a Whitlow linker (eg, tisagenlecleucel (tisa-cel) and ciltacabtagene autoleucel (cilta-cel)), the 1B4A1 antibody did not identify CAR T cells, despite plentiful circulating CAR T cells being detected with an anti-idiotype antibody or recombinant target protein (figure 3F,H). These findings highlight the potential of the 1B4A1 mAb as a clinical flow cytometry reagent for specific detection of engineered cells expressing a Whitlow linker.

sec.title: Novel anti-Whitlow mAbs can detect CAR T cells in situ in archival tissue by IHC
sec.p: The identification of CAR-engineered cells in FFPE tissue is a critical step towards improving our understanding of their in vivo activity and clinical outcomes. Four of the five mAbs that were reactive to Whitlow linker-containing CAR T cells by flow cytometry also detected cultured Whitlow-containing CAR T cells in FFPE cell pellets by IHC (online supplemental figure 6). Among these, 1B4A1 demonstrated particularly strong and specific binding of CAR T cells incorporating a Whitlow linker, while showing no reactivity toward unmodified human PBMCs or CAR T cells expressing the (G4S)4 linker (figure 4A).

sec.p: To assess the potential for reliable detection of CAR T cells in situ using the 1B4A1 mAb, we prepared admixtures of FMC63-Whitlow CAR T cells and untransduced human T cells and generated FFPE cell pellets. The fraction of CAR-positive cells was determined by IHC staining with 1B4A1 and compared with percentages obtained by flow cytometry immediately prior to cell fixation (figure 4B,C). We observed a strong correlation between the two methods (r²=0.966, p<0.0001), supporting the potential of 1B4A1 for accurate and quantitative detection of CAR T cells in FFPE samples.

Next, we tested whether the 1B4A1 antibody identifies CAR T cells in archival clinical FFPE tissue biopsies. We performed duplex IHC staining of a lymph node biopsy from a patient with large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL) treated in an early-phase clinical trial (NCT01865617) with CD19-targeting FMC63-Whitlow CAR T cells.13 Figure 4D shows fluorescent micrographs of staining with an anti-CD3 antibody (ThermoFisher, Cat# MA1-90582) and the 1B4A1 anti-Whitlow mAb. The merged image distinguishes T cells in the biopsy that do or do not express the CAR on their surface. Duplex staining of paired biopsies obtained pre-CAR and post-CAR T-cell infusion illustrates that CAR T cells identified by 1B4A1 are only observed in the post-infusion sample (figure 4E), as expected. The same optimized protocol was then used to stain a tissue microarray including 30 normal human tissues; we observed little or no background staining in any tissue (figure 4F), suggesting that the 1B4A1 mAb specifically identifies CAR T cells in situ and does not cross-react with normal human FFPE tissue.

To confirm the ability of 1B4A1 to detect different CAR T-cell products, we stained archival tumor biopsies from patients (n=10; online supplemental table 4) who were treated with different commercial Whitlow-containing CAR T cells. As expected, 1B4A1 staining did not identify CAR T cells in pretreatment samples (n=3). Figure 4G–I show representative post-infusion images from patients treated with liso-cel, axi-cel, and ide-cel, with CAR-expressing cells visualized in green. Notably, the total number of T cells, CAR T cells, and the proportion of T cells expressing CARs varied across the cohort (online supplemental table 4). Strong and specific staining of CAR-expressing cells was observed—not only in lymph node tissue but also in bone marrow particle preparations and gastrointestinal biopsies (figure 4I; online supplemental table 4).

sec.title: DNA barcoded anti-Whitlow mAbs enable spatial phenotyping of CAR T cells using highly multiplexed (high-plex) imaging
sec.p: Detection of CAR T cells in situ using high-plex spatial assays allows single-cell, multiparameter phenotyping of CAR T cells and their surrounding microenvironment. Barcoded antibodies to identify CAR-expressing cells are available for interrogation within fresh tissues (eg, Cell Signaling, Cat# 50265), yet there are no commercial reagents to our knowledge that specifically identify CAR-transduced cells for applications in situ. Therefore, we aimed to evaluate whether the 1B4A1 anti-Whitlow mAb could be equipped with a DNA barcode for high-plex spatial imaging.

To preserve its structural integrity and binding affinity, we employed click-chemistry-based custom site-specific methods targeting the antibody hinge region to barcode the 1B4A1 anti-Whitlow mAb. The barcoded antibody was successfully incorporated into a custom staining panel, which was then used to interrogate tissue biopsies on the PhenoCycler-Fusion instrument (Akoya Biosciences) (figure 5A; online supplemental table 2).

sec.p: We applied this panel to tumor biopsies obtained from two patients following liso-cel infusion for the treatment of LBCL: one patient who achieved a durable complete remission (figure 5B; online supplemental figure 7A), and another who experienced disease progression associated with loss of tumor CD19 expression (figure 5C; online supplemental figure 7B). CAR T cells were clearly identified by 1B4A1 in both tumor biopsies, including when in contact with CD19-positive lymphoma cells (figure 5B). The morphology of CAR T cells differed between the biopsies—those in the CD19-positive TME exhibited an irregular shape characteristic of active T cells (figure 5B), whereas CAR T cells in the CD19-negative tumor displayed round and inactive morphology (figure 5C).21 Furthermore, analyses of unsupervised clustering of these proteomic data (figure 5D) revealed that CAR T cells within the CD19-positive tumor milieu co-expressed GzmB and Ki-67 more frequently than those in the CD19 antigen-negative TME, where we also observed fewer interactions between the CD19-directed CAR T cells and Pax5-positive tumor cells (figure 5E,F). These data demonstrate the feasibility of incorporating barcoded anti-Whitlow mAbs into assays for high-plex CAR T-cell profiling, enabling deeper insights into their biology.

sec.title: Anti-Whitlow mAbs have distinct CAR stimulatory properties and can be leveraged for CAR T-cell manufacturing
sec.p: Due to their bivalency in native format, antibodies binding to the linker region within the scFv may crosslink CARs, thereby triggering CAR signaling.22 Given the differences in binding characteristics observed during flow cytometry staining and SPR testing, we reasoned that the abilities of individual mAbs to activate CAR T cells could differ.

To evaluate the activating potential of each anti-Whitlow mAb, we screened them using a Jurkat T-cell reporter line transduced to express one of several different CARs. This reporter line contains a GFP transgene knocked into the nur77 locus, enabling detection of early T-cell activation by GFP fluorescence. We found that the 1C3C3 mAb induced robust and specific activation of Jurkat reporter cells expressing an FMC63-Whitlow CAR, with the fraction of activated cells approaching levels seen with stimulation by target antigen expressed on the surface of live cells (figure 6A). This activation was dose-dependent and observed not only with plate-bound antibody but also when delivered in solution (online supplemental figure 8A and B). In contrast, other mAbs such as 1B4A1 showed minimal stimulatory activity, even at concentrations as high as 100 µg/mL. Notably, the stimulatory effects of 1C3C3 were not limited to the FMC63 scFv; nur77-GFP reporter activation was also demonstrated in reporter Jurkat cells transduced with the CD33-targeting 1H7 CAR, but only when the Whitlow linker was present in the CAR scFv (online supplemental figure 8C).

sec.p: We next evaluated the effects of these antibodies on CAR T cells generated from different healthy donors (n=2). The 1C3C3 antibody induced robust specific activation and expansion of CAR-expressing T cells, as evidenced by interferon-γ secretion, upregulation of Ki-67, and increased CAR T-cell accumulation. In contrast, the 1B4A1 mAb did not (figure 6B–D). These differences in activation potential among anti-Whitlow mAbs may be leveraged for different purposes, such as selective stimulation or binding of CAR-expressing cells without activation depending on the desired use.

Given their ability to selectively bind CAR-expressing cells, we considered that anti-Whitlow antibodies could serve as useful enrichment reagents during CAR T-cell manufacturing. To test this approach, we used 1B4A1, a non-activating mAb, to enrich FMC63-Whitlow CAR T cells using either magnetic bead separation or flow cytometry. From a range of dilutions of CAR-expressing cells admixed with untransduced T cells, 1B4A1 enabled consistent enrichment of CAR T cells, achieving a mean CAR T-cell purity of 92.12% (SD 4.6%) following magnetic bead purification and 94.35% (SD 0.816%) by FACS (figure 6E,F).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The ability to study CAR T cells in clinical samples will be crucial to understand factors that influence the outcomes of these immunotherapies.23,26 To address this, we generated five murine mAbs targeting the Whitlow linker peptide contained within the scFv of the CAR in most commercially available CAR T-cell products. Our mAb discovery campaign was unique in its design to generate reagents capable of detecting CAR-engineered cells in both fresh and fixed tissues. Four of these mAbs were confirmed by SPR to specifically bind the Whitlow peptide and exhibited a range of binding affinities that were preserved in rank when the peptide was presented within the context of a full scFv recombinant protein.

Structural modeling revealed that most of the mAb Fv regions possess a deep, negatively charged cleft that provides high degrees of both shape and electrostatic complementarity to peptides, effectively cradling the Whitlow linker.27 Notably, the predicted net surface charge of each Fv is low (<+4), reducing the likelihood of nonspecific interactions due to polyreactivity, and consistent with the high specificity of the anti-Whitlow mAbs for Whitlow linker-containing CARs observed in our assays.28

All five mAbs specifically detect CAR T cells incorporating a Whitlow peptide within the scFv by flow cytometry with 1B4A1 demonstrating the most consistent performance across scFvs targeting different antigens. Side-by-side comparisons of 1B4A1 with anti-FMC63 idiotype antibodies and recombinant protein-based detection methods revealed comparable performance in patient-derived peripheral blood samples. This supports its use for monitoring CAR T-cell abundance and phenotype in peripheral blood, fresh tissues and liquid specimens (eg, cerebrospinal fluid), enabling insights into therapeutic efficacy and potential toxicities.1011 13 29,31

The use of non-standardized metrics and limited availability of quantitative data in correlative analyses of CAR T cells currently hinders meaningful comparisons across clinical trials, between different CAR constructs, and in routine clinical practice. This challenge is particularly critical in early-phase clinical trials, where detailed analysis of CAR T-cell kinetics can inform key aspects of trial design, such as dosing, scheduling, and patient selection, to optimize therapeutic outcomes.32 Because anti-Whitlow mAbs target the linker sequence rather than the antigen-binding site, they could potentially be used to develop standardized clinical assays for CAR T-cell detection employable across a range of CAR T-cell products and would also be expected to detect CARs engineered into other immune cells, such as natural killer cells.3032,34

An imperfect correlation between clinical response and peak peripheral blood CAR T-cell counts and phenotype has led to increasing investigation into the activity and interactions of these cells within the TME.14 35 36 Anti-Whitlow mAbs enable the interrogation of CAR T cells in situ, and 1B4A1 performed best. It demonstrated high-quality staining and accurate quantification of CAR T cells in biopsies from patients treated with various commercial CAR T-cell products and in multiple tissue types. As an IHC detection reagent, this can be developed into a low-cost clinical assay, demonstrating the presence and location of CAR-engineered cells within the TME and differentiating them from their untransduced counterparts. Furthermore, it is the first antibody to our knowledge to be successfully barcoded to enable the use of high-plex proteomics platforms to study CAR-engineered cells in situ, their phenotype and spatial interactions with other cell types. As a proof of concept, we quantified activated CAR T cells within the TME of patients with LBCL treated with liso-cel. Activated CAR T cells with distinct morphology and co-expression of GzmB and Ki-67 were present in increased abundance and proximal to CD19-expressing tumor cells early after CAR T-cell infusion. Conversely, in a patient who developed progressive lymphoma with decreased CD19 expression, the abundance of these activated CAR T cells and their engagement with viable tumor cells in the TME were significantly reduced. These findings require further validation but highlight the use case for these antibodies in spatial proteomics and we are applying them in other multiomic platforms where oligo-tagged antibodies are required, such as cellular indexing of transcriptomes and epitopes by sequencing (CITE-seq).37 38

In addition to identifying CAR-engineered cells, anti-Whitlow mAbs can be used to selectively isolate CAR-expressing cells from mixed populations. Furthermore, the distinct properties of each mAb in native format may enable tailored strategies for enrichment and expansion of CAR-engineered cells. In this report, we demonstrate that the non-stimulatory 1B4A1 clone can efficiently purify CAR-expressing cells using both FACS and magnetic bead-based methods that can be readily integrated into CAR T-cell manufacturing procedures to improve product purity.

One of the anti-Whitlow mAbs, 1C3C3, exhibited striking capacity to selectively activate Whitlow linker-containing CAR T cells. Further investigation is needed to determine whether the mechanism of CAR T-cell stimulation by this antibody mirrors or differs from activation induced by antigen-expressing cells. The 1C3C3 mAb could be adapted as a tool to assess CAR T-cell functionality in vitro, both during preclinical development and as a post-manufacturing quality control assay. More intriguingly, if selective CAR T-cell expansion can be achieved without inducing exhaustion, 1C3C3 may offer a novel approach for in vitro expansion or even in vivo modulation of CAR T-cell activity.

We have developed and characterized a panel of anti-Whitlow mAbs with broad utility for the detection, functional assessment, and enrichment of CAR-engineered cells. These reagents address key limitations in current detection and monitoring approaches by enabling target antigen-agnostic identification of CAR T cells across multiple platforms, including flow cytometry, IHC, and high-plex proteomics. Their application spans preclinical development, in vitro quality control, standardized clinical assays, and clinical correlative studies—extending even to the TME, where they enable spatially resolved CAR T-cell profiling. The distinct functional properties of individual mAbs also present opportunities for CAR T-cell manufacturing optimization and potentially, therapeutic modulation. These anti-Whitlow binding reagents represent a versatile and scalable resource to support the continued advancement of both the research and clinical applications of CAR-engineered cells.
